The four conditions under which taking part in the transaction pays, with the documented record of leboncoin, Kleinanzeigen, Marktplaats, OLX, Vinted and eBay, and the payment models (provider marketplace product, specialist payment institution, own licence, off-platform).

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given three transaction proposals and an unmatched clearing balance, the reader decides each and names what must come first.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your protected-payment service for second-hand goods earns a 7.4% take rate, but about €2.3 million of items in its clearing account match no order at month-end. Three proposals arrive: launch it in one more country of the same goods marketplace, add a secure payment for €20,000 private car sales, and hold rental deposits for a property portal. Using only this chapter: what do you decide for each, and what comes first?
acceptance_criteria.expected: First, the transaction platform: an order context that owns availability and timers, a shipping context, a dispute case service and a transaction ledger that receives order and money events, so every amount is traceable and DAC7 aggregates come from the ledger. The new country is approved on that platform, since all four conditions hold. Car payment fails on price and on professional sellers: at most a narrow design study (short hold around a handover, flat fee, payee verification). Rental deposits are declined as a Forced Fit: a goods checkout is not a rental product, and the fraud is better answered upstream by identity checks and messaging warnings.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Why classifieds stayed out of the money and why the European horizontals moved in for some categories; the three terms the chapter owns; its question and its link to RECONCILED; then the Veldmark forum's three proposals and clearing account, concepts, when to take part, payment models, the transaction platform's contexts and state machine, two Safe Deal orders, the forum's decisions, trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, the Chief Architect's view and questions. Evidence: annual reports and help pages of Adevinta, Kleinanzeigen, OLX, Vinted and eBay, Which?, provider documentation, the PSD2 directive, and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: When and how should a classifieds marketplace move into transactions, and what does it take architecturally?
thesis.claim: A classifieds marketplace should take part in the transaction per category, not per brand, and only where the item ships, the price is moderate (tens to a few hundred euros), the buyer's main fear is non-delivery and the sale is otherwise between strangers, gated as configuration per country and category so it can be switched off; a licensed provider's marketplace product should hold the money and verify payees, while the marketplace owns six contexts beside the listing core (order with availability and timers, payment edge, fees, shipping, buyer protection and disputes, and the transaction ledger with tax reporting), and the ledger, release rules and dispute desk ship with the checkout rather than after it.
thesis.disputed_by: Two opposite views: that a classifieds marketplace should stay out of payments entirely to remain cheap to run and free of payment regulation, or that it should make every brand and category transactional to capture a take rate, launching the checkout as a product feature and adding the ledger and dispute handling once volume justifies them.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this records the pivot per country and category in the marketplace profile register, gives no category protected payment without a named owner for disputes, reconciliation and DAC7, funds the transaction platform before any new country launches on it, keeps the order, the ledger and the seller's verification outcome in the marketplace's own systems with provider identifiers as references, and judges the pivot by protected share of eligible sales, dispute rate, buyer-protection losses as a share of GMV and month-end reconciliation breaks.
thesis.how_why: Safe Deal processed 11.6 million orders worth about €1.02 billion in 2026 for €75 million of revenue, a 7.4% take rate with buyer-protection losses of about €4.1 million, yet at the December 2026 month-end about €2.3 million sat unmatched in a clearing account: refunds after payouts, label charges netted from settlements and partial refunds agreed in chat had no ledger to land in. The four conditions sorted the September 2027 proposals: Portugal approved on the rebuilt platform; Motorvane narrowed to a design study, since a 5% fee on the €21,900 Golf would be about €1,095; Hearthly's rental deposits declined as a Forced Fit. leboncoin, Kleinanzeigen and Marktplaats added payments for goods, not cars or homes, and OLX scaled its pay-and-ship flow back.

supporting_claims.claim: Taking part in the transaction pays only where four conditions hold together (the item ships, the price is moderate, the buyer's main fear is non-delivery or misdescription, the sale is otherwise between strangers), so the pivot is decided per country and category and held as configuration that can be switched off, as the European horizontals' record shows.

A licensed provider's marketplace product should hold the money and verify payees: an own licence pays only for payment-first marketplaces at very large volume, staying out gives up the trust and observability gains, and collecting for both parties does not fit the PSD2 commercial-agent exclusion.

Even with a provider holding the money, the marketplace owns six contexts beside the listing core (order with availability and timers, payment edge, fees and pricing, shipping, buyer protection and disputes, transaction ledger and reporting), and the order, not the listing, becomes the system of record for the sale.

Buyer protection is a liability with a product attached: evidence-based release rules, a dispute case desk, a loss provision and a ledger that explains every amount must ship with the checkout, or the pivot produces unreconciled money, as Safe Deal's €2.3 million clearing balance shows.

Moving money on-platform turns on DAC7 reporting, trader-traceability and consumer-law duties and the provider's payment regulation, and makes the protected-payment brand a phishing target, so the launch decision is also a tax-reporting and safety decision.

At group scale the transaction platform is shared only among the profiles that use it, with country parts as adapters, the provider treated as a strategic dependency whose identifiers are references, named owners for disputes, reconciliation and DAC7, and the pivot judged on trust and money metrics together.

role.contribution: Follows the contact into the deal: decides where the marketplace takes part in the transaction and what it must then own, and adds the transactional revenue line the next chapter compares with the others.

additional_patterns.applies_to: scene to forum: the forum's three proposals and clearing account are posed first and decided only after the framework is built
trade-offs, verticals, failure-modes, ca-view, questions: the book's standard judging sections

flow.rationale: Each section supplies what the next one needs. The scene poses the decisions; the concepts give the terms every later section uses; the four conditions decide whether to take part before the payment models decide who holds the money, since a category that fails the conditions needs no model; the architecture then specifies what the marketplace owns once a provider holds the money; the two orders exercise that architecture, and only then can the forum's decisions be read as applications of conditions and platform together. Putting the architecture before the conditions would design a platform before the reader knows where it should run; putting the forum's decisions straight after the scene would give verdicts with no framework behind them. The judging sections follow the decisions they generalize.

hook.content: For twenty years, the classifieds bargain was simple: the platform finds the buyer, and the buyer and seller sort out the money themselves. That bargain kept classifieds cheap to run and free of payment regulation, and it left the moment money changes hands entirely outside the platform's control.

bridge.from_reader_world: The classifieds model the reader knows from Parts I to V and from messaging-and-leads: the marketplace's job ends at the contact, and advance-payment scams and fake payment links land in the gap it leaves.
bridge.to_topic: Since about 2017 the large European horizontals have moved into that moment for some categories, so an offer accepted in chat now leaves a choice: step aside, or carry the deal through payment, shipping and buyer protection; the question is when, and what the platform must then own.

thesis_statement.text: The transactional pivot is a category decision, not a brand decision, gated in configuration; a licensed partner holds the money while the marketplace owns everything around it; and buyer protection is a liability whose ledger, release rules and dispute desk ship with the checkout.

sections.heading: Concepts: What Changes When the Platform Takes Part in the Sale
sections.controlling_idea: Taking part in the sale moves a category from a job that ends at the contact to one that ends at payment and delivery, and brings terms (order, marketplace payments, PSP, payee verification, hold and release, payout, merchant of record, buyer protection, dispute versus chargeback, PUDO) and two separations the rest of the chapter relies on.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the vocabulary and the two separations (money from risk, order from listing) on which the payment models and the contexts rest.

flow.rationale: The change in the marketplace's job first, then the terms it brings, then the two separations that only make sense once order, PSP and buyer protection are defined.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The transactional pivot moves a category from a job that ends at the contact to one that ends when payment and delivery are complete, and brings ten terms the classifieds side has rarely needed.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The order is a separate aggregate from the listing: a listing can have many conversations and orders, an order has one buyer, one seller and one price, and money belongs to the order.

sections.heading: When to Take Part in the Transaction
sections.controlling_idea: The pivot pays where four conditions hold together, and the dated record of the European horizontals (category-gated launches, margin-diluting economics and the trust case) supports deciding it per category.

advances_thesis.how: States the four conditions and the public evidence for gating the pivot per category.

transition_in.introduces: The first decision they serve: whether to take part at all.

flow.rationale: The conditions are asserted first so the evidence has something to support; the evidence runs from what companies did (category gating) through what it cost (economics) to why it is still worth it (trust); the rule of thumb and figure close the section once the reader has the reasons.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The documented record suggests the pivot pays where four conditions hold together: the item ships, the price is moderate, the buyer's main fear is non-delivery or misdescription, and the sale is otherwise between strangers.

evidence.what: Four conditions, each with why it matters, strong fit and weak fit (phones and clothes versus sofas, cars and homes; tens to a few hundred euros versus tens of thousands; private distance purchases versus professional sellers; C2C goods versus dealer and agency sales).
evidence.shows: Turns the conditions into a test a reader can apply to any category.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Category gating is what the European horizontals did: leboncoin, Marktplaats and Kleinanzeigen launched payments for selected goods categories, and mobile.de earned essentially no transactional revenue.

evidence.what: Adevinta Annual Report 2019 (leboncoin, 2019); Marktplaats 2017, 2019; eBay Kleinanzeigen Sicher bezahlen, October 2020, initially toys, phones, PCs and notebooks (onlinemarketing.de, 2020); mobile.de 2023 (Adevinta Annual Report 2023).
evidence.shows: Shows companies gated the pivot by category, not by brand.

transition_in.introduces: Dated evidence that companies applied them by category.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The economics are documented too: transactional revenue grows but dilutes margin and adds direct costs, and OLX scaled its pay-and-ship flow back.

evidence.what: Adevinta transactional revenue €103 million in 2023, about 6% of group revenue; France EBITDA margin down two points; direct costs from payment and shipping providers; OLX Pay&Ship (OLX Tech, 2023) and Prosus' de-prioritisation of pay-and-ship in Europe (FY25, 2025).
evidence.shows: Shows the pivot has a cost, and that a large operator retreated from it.

transition_in.carries_over: Evidence of how the pivot was gated.
transition_in.introduces: Evidence of what it costs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The trust case is the strongest argument: in-platform payment turns an unrecoverable push-payment fraud into a dispute the platform can resolve.

evidence.what: Which? (December 2024): eBay, Vinted, Depop, Shpock, Preloved and Amazon Marketplace offered some buyer protection; Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree and Nextdoor did not, and a quarter of their buyers believed theirs did.
evidence.shows: Shows buyers expect protection and that it changes what happens after a scam; links the pivot to trust-and-safety-architecture.

transition_in.introduces: The benefit that justifies them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The author's rule of thumb is to take part where the platform's presence removes a fear that stops sales, and stay out where professionals already carry that fear.

evidence.what: Figure 1: a four-layer sieve that passes small shippable goods to protected payment and diverts cars and homes to contact only.
evidence.shows: Shows the four conditions as one per-category decision.

transition_in.introduces: The rule the author draws from them.

sections.heading: Payment Models: Who Holds the Money
sections.controlling_idea: A marketplace in the EU can use a licensed provider's marketplace product, hold a licence itself or stay out of the flow of funds, and for a classifieds group the provider's product is the normal answer.

advances_thesis.how: Compares the payment models with documented provider behavior and concludes for the provider's marketplace product.

transition_in.introduces: The next decision once a category qualifies: who holds the money.

flow.rationale: The three options are introduced, then each is described in the order classifieds groups use them (provider product, specialist institutions, own licence, staying out), with the legal reason against the improvised fourth option; the comparison table follows once each row has been explained, and Veldmark's choice ends the section.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A marketplace that wants to collect from buyers and pay sellers in the EU has three basic options (a licensed provider's marketplace product, its own licence, or staying out of the flow of funds); the comparison counts five models because it splits the first by merchant of record and gives specialist institutions their own row; classifieds groups have used the first.
A licensed provider's marketplace product onboards and verifies sellers, collects, holds, splits and pays out, and its charge type decides who carries refunds and chargebacks first.

evidence.what: Adyen documentation: onboard users, process payments, pay out; verify users; split payments, deduct costs, hold funds until payout. Stripe Connect: direct charges, destination charges, separate charges and transfers; for the latter two 'refunds and chargebacks reduce your platform's balance'.
evidence.shows: Shows what the provider does and that the platform still carries refunds under some charge types.

transition_in.introduces: How a provider's marketplace product works.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Specialist marketplace payment institutions serve the same need, and the classifieds record shows providers changing over time.

evidence.what: Online Payment Platform carried Marktplaats' flow in 2017 and eBay Kleinanzeigen's in 2020 (Worldline, 2022; t3n, 2023); Kleinanzeigen's help page named Adyen in October 2026, change date not public; leboncoin trusted third party since 2018 with Adyen (Wikipedia, 2026).
evidence.shows: Shows the provider model in use at the main European horizontals, with dated provider claims.

transition_in.introduces: Specialist institutions doing the same job.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Holding a licence yourself brings safeguarding, capital, supervision and a ledger of your own, and it pays only when payments are the core of the product at large volume.

evidence.what: Vinted Pay: e-money licence from the Bank of Lithuania (2023), members moved onto its wallet from January 2026, 'expected to reduce payment-related costs and dependencies' (Vinted, 2026).
evidence.shows: Shows the conditions under which a marketplace takes the licence route.

transition_in.introduces: Holding one yourself.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Staying out of the flow of funds avoids payment regulation and DAC7 but gives up the trust and observability gains, and collecting for both sides without a licence does not fit PSD2's commercial-agent exclusion.

evidence.what: Directive (EU) 2015/2366 Art. 3(b): payments 'through a commercial agent authorised via an agreement' to act for only the payer or only the payee; a question for counsel, not a design default (callout).
evidence.shows: Explains why 'we just collect and pass it on' is not a fourth option.

transition_in.introduces: The opposite end: no part in the money.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The comparison table counts five models, because the provider option appears twice (platform or seller as merchant of record) and the specialist institutions get their own row, and they differ in who holds funds, who verifies payees and who loses first.

evidence.what: Five rows (provider product with the platform as merchant; provider product with the seller as merchant; specialist institution; own licence; off-platform) by who holds funds, verifies payees, carries chargebacks first, what the marketplace owns and where each fits.
evidence.shows: Lets the reader place any marketplace's choice and see what it still owns in each.

transition_in.carries_over: The three options described one by one.
transition_in.introduces: All of them side by side.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark chose the first row, so Safe Deal conforms to Adyen's model and translates only where an order meets a listing.

evidence.what: bounded-contexts records the Safe Deal context conforming to Adyen's accounts, balances and payouts.
evidence.shows: Shows the conformist relationship the provider choice creates, which the Chief Architect's view returns to.

transition_in.introduces: Veldmark's row and its consequence.

sections.heading: Architecture: The Transaction Platform
sections.controlling_idea: A transactional pivot adds six bounded contexts beside the listing core, and their design rules (order-owned availability, timed states, release as a decision, reconciled money states, shipping events as evidence, a dispute case desk, a ledger with per-seller aggregates and the regulatory switches) decide whether the pivot can be operated.

advances_thesis.how: Specifies what the marketplace owns even with a provider holding the money, and the rules that make protection operable and reportable.

transition_in.introduces: What the marketplace must still own and build.

additional_patterns.applies_to: p26 to p35: availability and the state machine (order) first, then shipping whose events feed release, then disputes and protection that use those events, then the ledger that records all of it, then the obligations the ledger serves

flow.rationale: The six contexts are shown whole first, then each is opened in the order its inputs become available: the order's availability and states, the shipping events that release depends on, the disputes that hold release, the ledger that records every amount, and the regulatory duties computed from the ledger. Describing the ledger before the order and shipping events would leave nothing for it to record.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A provider holding the money does not take the transaction off the marketplace's hands: the public flows of Kleinanzeigen and Marktplaats show the marketplace owning the offer and acceptance, fee pricing, labels and tracking, the release timer and disputes.

evidence.what: The INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED callout on Kleinanzeigen's and Marktplaats' public flows as a plausible reference architecture.
evidence.shows: Shows how much of a provider-held transaction stays with the marketplace, labelled as inference rather than a description of either company's systems.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Built out, those responsibilities become six bounded contexts beside the listing core, none of which belongs inside the listing service.

evidence.what: Order, payment edge, fees and pricing, shipping, buyer protection and disputes, transaction ledger and reporting, each with what it owns, key events and what it must not own.
evidence.shows: Gives each responsibility one owner and keeps money and release out of the listing.

evidence.what: Figure 2: the transaction platform beside the listing core; the ledger receives both order and money events.
evidence.shows: Shows the contexts' relationships and that finance and tax reporting come from one record.

transition_in.carries_over: The responsibilities the marketplace keeps in the public flows.
transition_in.introduces: The six bounded contexts they become.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The order must own availability: it reserves the listing atomically when payment is committed, and the reservation must time out.

evidence.what: At Tradeyard a Safe Deal order emits ListingReserved; search shows a badge and alerts stop; an unpaid or uncollected order must release the listing or it becomes Ghost Inventory in reverse.
evidence.shows: Shows the double sale prevented and the opposite failure avoided.

transition_in.carries_over: The order context in the table.
transition_in.introduces: Its first rule, against the most common integration bug.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: When the order completes, the sale must reach every copy of the listing; one copy that misses it keeps selling an item that is gone, and In Practice follows Femke's bike to the copy that missed it.

evidence.what: Search, saved-search alerts, digests, recommendations and sitemaps as copies of the listing; a forward pointer to the bike order in In Practice.
evidence.shows: Shows that completion is an event every downstream copy must consume, and sets up the example without telling its outcome early.

transition_in.carries_over: The reservation while the order is open.
transition_in.introduces: What happens when the order completes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Figure 3 draws the order's whole life (four waiting states with deadlines, exits that return money and release the listing, and chargebacks that reopen a completed order), and four design rules govern that life: every waiting state has a timer and an owner, release is a decision, money states are reconciled with order states, and states after completion are first-class.

evidence.what: Figure 3: a protected-payment order for goods, with deadlines on waiting states and chargebacks after completion.
evidence.shows: Shows the states the rules govern.

evidence.what: Kleinanzeigen: automatic payment to the seller after 14 days without confirmation; Marktplaats' 2022 successor paid on day 8 without complaints (AVROTROS Radar, 2022); release holds need a DSA statement of reasons; provider webhooks arrive at least once and out of order.
evidence.shows: Shows that documented flows use timers and that release and reconciliation are design decisions.

transition_in.introduces: The order's whole life as Figure 3 draws it, and the rules that govern it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shipping turns a marketplace into a logistics integrator at a scale now visible in carrier choices, PUDO networks and sustainability reporting.

evidence.what: Kleinanzeigen: DHL in four sizes and Hermes in four; Vinted: more than 500,000 PUDO points and Vinted Go in five countries (2026); Adevinta's 2025 report on shipment-driven emissions for five marketplaces.
evidence.shows: Shows how much logistics a protected-payment flow brings with it.

transition_in.introduces: The shipping context that feeds its release decision.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The shipping context needs carrier adapters, a normalized tracking-event model, label pricing, address validation and a lost-parcel policy, and its events are the evidence protection rests on.

transition_in.introduces: What the shipping context must therefore contain, and why event timeliness is a reliability requirement.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Shipping also changes discovery: distance becomes a cost input, and a fee that varies per item must be computed on the search and listing read path.

evidence.what: Vinted UK price list (October 2026): the buyer fee varies with 'item characteristics, order value, order type'; location-and-geo.
evidence.shows: Shows that fee pricing reaches the read path, not only the checkout.

transition_in.introduces: Its effect on search and listing pages.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A dispute desk is a case-management system with money attached, best built as a shared capability with an anti-corruption layer per marketplace and a canonical case model.

evidence.what: Kleinanzeigen's five covered cases (2026); Adevinta's reusable dispute back office ingesting per-marketplace events through Kafka, SQS or REST, 'We couldn't hardcode anything… or make any assumptions' (2023).
evidence.shows: Shows what a desk handles and that a cross-marketplace design is documented.

transition_in.introduces: The desk that uses them when a buyer disputes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A protection promise is a liability that must be provisioned, measured per category and priced into the fee.

evidence.what: eBay Form 10-K for 2025: transaction losses consist 'primarily of losses resulting from our buyer protection programs, chargebacks'.
evidence.shows: Shows that a large marketplace reports protection as a loss line.

transition_in.introduces: The money those decisions cost.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every amount in an order must be explainable later, which needs RECONCILED's normalization and three-way match plus per-seller balances and per-seller, per-period aggregates.

evidence.what: payments-to-ledger and designing-financial-ledgers; provider settlement reports are net, batched and late.
evidence.shows: Shows why reconciliation is designed, and what a marketplace adds to the sibling book's design.

transition_in.introduces: The ledger that records them with every other amount.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Moving money on-platform turns on DAC7 seller reporting, consumer and trader-traceability duties, and payment regulation through the provider.

evidence.what: DAC7: report seller identity, account identifiers and consideration per quarter; excluded below 30 sales and €2,000 (Belastingdienst); the launch is also a tax-reporting decision; DSA trader traceability; provider onboarding and limits as product constraints.
evidence.shows: Shows the obligations the ledger's aggregates serve and why they start on day one.

transition_in.introduces: The obligations that require them.

sections.heading: In Practice: Two Safe Deal Orders
sections.controlling_idea: Two Safe Deal orders, a pay-at-pickup bike and a shipped lens with a dispute, show every context producing events and every amount needing a ledger line.

advances_thesis.how: Walks the design through two orders with ledger figures and shows the phishing risk and the cost of a missing ledger.

transition_in.introduces: Two orders that exercise it.

flow.rationale: Femke's story is told in time order: the fake buyer on Sunday evening first, so the reader meets the risk the brand attracts before the real order; then the Monday pay-at-pickup order, what its steps record, and the digest that missed its sale (the example the Architecture section pointed to); then a shipped order with a dispute that touches every context and ends on the ledger lines the clearing account lacked. The simpler order comes first so the reader knows the contexts' steps before a dispute complicates them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Femke's bike listing drew a fake buyer within half an hour, showing that a protected-payment brand is the scammer's favorite disguise, so the countermeasure belongs in the message safety gate, not the payment platform.

evidence.what: At 20:11 on Sunday a fake Safe Deal link on a domain registered that day reached Femke; about 41,000 payment-link phishing reports in NL and BE in 2026; messaging-and-leads' gate; Fast Mail for Fraudsters.
evidence.shows: Shows the safety cost a pivot brings with its brand.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Femke's €225 bike order shows pay at pickup: the buyer pays in the app before the meeting, the money is held, and the seller receives it at the handover.

evidence.what: Mon 8 March 2027: 14:01 offer accepted, fee €11.95; 14:02 €236.95 paid by iDEAL, listing reserved; other conversations told; 18:08 handover code releases €225; 18:10 sold; Tuesday 07:00 the digest assembled at 17:30 Monday still features the bike to 214 users; Tuesday payout.
evidence.shows: Shows each context's step and the money in it.

transition_in.carries_over: The fake buyer on Sunday evening.
transition_in.introduces: The real sale on Monday.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The bike order shows what each part records: the handover code is the release event that limits coverage, Adyen's prior verification makes Femke payable, and the buyer-paid fee keeps her DAC7 consideration at €225.

evidence.what: payee.verified claim in Veldmark ID; four Safe Deal sales in 2027 totaling €610, so Femke is an excluded seller.
evidence.shows: Shows release, verification and tax reporting at the level of one seller.

transition_in.introduces: What its steps mean for release, verification and tax.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Tuesday digest row is the Architecture section's propagation rule broken: the bike sold at 18:10 and left search a minute later, but a digest assembled at 17:30 from an older replica snapshot and not re-checked still featured it to 214 users.

evidence.what: Sold 18:10 Monday 8 March 2027, removed from search 18:11; the 07:00 Tuesday digest assembled at 17:30 Monday from a MySQL replica snapshot, not re-checked, went to 214 users.
evidence.shows: Shows that completion is an event every downstream copy must consume.

transition_in.carries_over: The bike order's timeline and what its steps record.
transition_in.introduces: The table's Tuesday digest row as the propagation rule broken.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A shipped €60 lens order with a dispute exercises every context, from label and PUDO through the dispute window to a partial refund and payout.

evidence.what: 13 to 20 April 2027, Antwerp buyer, Ghent seller: €70.65 paid (€60 + €3.70 fee + €6.95 label); hand-in within three days; two-day dispute window; dispute over a scratch; €15 partial refund; €45 payout; fee not refunded; label €6.95 charged against about €5.20 carrier cost.
evidence.shows: Shows the timers, evidence and amounts of a shipped order.

transition_in.carries_over: A local order released at the handover and the digest that missed its sale.
transition_in.introduces: A shipped order with a dispute.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every step of the lens order produced an event and every amount has a ledger line, the link the December 2026 clearing balance lacked because partial refunds before 2027 were agreed in chat and executed manually.

evidence.what: Figure 4: unmatched items in a clearing bin versus a ledger where each line links to an order event.
evidence.shows: Shows the difference the event-to-ledger design makes.

transition_in.introduces: The ledger lines they produce and why clearing filled up before 2027.

sections.heading: The Architecture Advice Forum's Decisions
sections.controlling_idea: Applying the four conditions and the architecture, the forum approved Portugal on the target platform, narrowed Motorvane to a design study, declined Hearthly's deposits as The Forced Fit, and funded the transaction platform first.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the framework producing approve, narrow and decline outcomes and the ledger funded before growth.

transition_in.carries_over: The forum's three proposals and the clearing account from the scene, and the framework since built.
transition_in.introduces: The forum's decisions.

flow.rationale: Each problem the scene posed is resolved in the order the scene listed it, from the clearest fit to the clearest misfit, and the fourth item, the clearing account, is resolved last because the Portugal approval depends on it; deciding the platform first would announce a funding decision before the reader sees which proposal needs it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: On 22 September 2027 the forum applied the four conditions and the architecture to each proposal.

Safe Deal Portugal was approved for Q3 2028 on the target platform, not on the 2024 design that serves Safe Deal's first three countries, because all four conditions hold, and it waits for the platform work.

evidence.what: Local payment methods and two national carrier and PUDO networks through new adapters; same Tradeyard B.V. contract with Adyen; DAC7 through the existing Dutch filing.
evidence.shows: Shows an approval that reuses the platform and its reporting.

transition_in.introduces: The first proposal.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Motorvane's private car payment fails on price and professional sellers, so the forum approved only a narrow design study for a secure handover.

evidence.what: A 5% fee on the Essen Golf's €21,900 would be about €1,095; most listings from dealers; funds held at most 72 hours, flat buyer fee, handover code, proof-of-person payee verification; decision Q2 2028; fraud-prevention controls meanwhile.
evidence.shows: Shows a narrowed outcome where conditions fail.

transition_in.carries_over: A proposal where all conditions hold.
transition_in.introduces: One where two fail.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Hearthly's protected deposits were declined as The Forced Fit, because a rental deposit is part of a lease, and the Barcelona ring is better answered upstream.

evidence.what: Proof of person with name match for private landlords in Spain from Q4 2027 (identity-and-verification); messaging warnings when a deposit is requested before a viewing.
evidence.shows: Shows a decline and the alternative controls.

transition_in.introduces: A declined one.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The transaction platform was funded first, with end-2028 targets for traceability, unmatched clearing and DAC7.

evidence.what: Order service owning availability and timers, shipping with normalized tracking, dispute cases on shared trust-and-safety case management, ledger feeding group finance; every amount traceable order to bank; unmatched clearing under €100,000 at any month-end; DAC7 aggregates from the ledger.
evidence.shows: Shows the ledger shipped before growth, answering Ingrid's fourth item.

transition_in.carries_over: Three proposal decisions, one of which waits for the platform.
transition_in.introduces: The platform decision they depend on.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.controlling_idea: The transaction platform's main decisions each have an option that is right under stated conditions, with buyer-paid fees and sharing across countries the two that need most judgement.

advances_thesis.how: Places the recommended choices among their alternatives and says when each alternative is right.

transition_in.introduces: The general alternatives behind them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The forum's decisions fit Veldmark and another marketplace could decide otherwise: eight decisions shape any transaction platform, each with two options right under different conditions, the first two restating the payment models as choices.

evidence.what: Who holds funds; merchant of record; release rule; fee payer; fee shape; shipping; scope of a shared platform; pivot depth, each with when to prefer A or B.
evidence.shows: Lets the reader choose per decision rather than adopt a package.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Buyer-paid fees keep selling free and put the price at the moment of highest intent, as Vinted's and Marktplaats' fees show.

evidence.what: Vinted UK price list (October 2026): 'the Vinted fee', paid at checkout, 'usually 3% to 8% + £0.3 to £0.8'; Marktplaats 2017 2% + €0.40 (RetailTrends), 2022 successor 5% (AVROTROS Radar).
evidence.shows: Shows the buyer-paid model in documented use and its price range.

transition_in.introduces: Why buyer-paid fees are usually chosen.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Sharing the transaction platform across countries is attractive but most exposed to local differences, as Adevinta's move from shared to local ownership shows.

evidence.what: Adevinta 2023 plan to stop duplicating 'the full transactional journey'; 2025 decentralization.
evidence.shows: Shows the sharing trade-off in both directions.

transition_in.carries_over: A row with a clear default.
transition_in.introduces: A row that needs judgement.

sections.heading: Vertical Differences
sections.controlling_idea: The pivot is common for general goods and recommerce and rare elsewhere, and automotive shows that transactional state on a professional's inventory must be opt-in, configurable and reversible.

advances_thesis.how: Applies the four conditions across verticals and shows the professional pushback.

transition_in.introduces: Differences by vertical.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The verticals differ in whether the pivot happens at all, what is paid on the platform, who holds funds and which fear protection answers.

evidence.what: General goods, real estate, automotive, recommerce and jobs by whether the pivot is common, what is paid, who holds funds, the fear protection answers and the typical failure.
evidence.shows: Shows the four conditions holding for goods and failing for property and cars.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Autotrader's Deal Builder shows professionals pushing back when transactional state is placed on their inventory, so such state must be opt-in, configurable and reversible.

evidence.what: Autotrader FY26 results (2026): fall in retailer forecourts partly attributed to 'concerns with the speed and nature of our Deal Builder product roll-out'; auto-rollout paused; 'request a reservation' without buyer payment (Car Dealer Magazine, December 2025).
evidence.shows: Shows the professional side of the trade-off in dated evidence.

transition_in.introduces: Automotive as the case.

sections.heading: Failure Modes
sections.controlling_idea: Nine failure modes, from a checkout shipped before its ledger to the goods checkout forced onto other verticals, are the design rules of the chapter broken one at a time.

advances_thesis.how: Shows what happens when each rule of the chapter is skipped.

transition_in.carries_over: How the design and its alternatives should be chosen.
transition_in.introduces: What goes wrong when they are not.

flow.rationale: The ledger failure Veldmark actually suffered comes first; then the failures of the order's life (release, double sale, propagation, disputes), then those that come from outside the order (phishing, tax, provider), and the vertical misfit last because it returns to the per-category decision. Each item names the symptom of a rule set out earlier; out of this order the reader would meet external failures before the order's own life that they depend on.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The design rules and choices work only when made on purpose; the first of nine failures, the one Veldmark met, is the checkout shipping before the ledger, so the first month-end finds refunds, label charges and chargebacks unmatched and the ledger belongs in the launch criteria.

advances_thesis.how: Names a failure the corresponding design rule prevents.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Release by timer only pays scammers who never ship, so release should depend on delivery and the dispute window with a fraud hold.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The double sale happens when the listing stays available during an order, so the order must reserve atomically with an expiry.

transition_in.introduces: Another failure mode.

advances_thesis.how: Names a failure the corresponding design rule prevents.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A sale that does not reach every copy of the listing creates Ghost Inventory, as the bike in the Tuesday digest shows.

advances_thesis.how: Names a failure the corresponding design rule prevents.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Disputes handled by e-mail are inconsistent and leave no data to price protection, so a desk needs cases, evidence, decision codes and service levels.

transition_in.introduces: Another failure mode.

advances_thesis.how: Names a failure the corresponding design rule prevents.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Phishing that imitates the protected-payment flow follows every launch, so messaging must treat brand-imitating links as high risk.

advances_thesis.how: Names a failure the corresponding design rule prevents.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Discovering DAC7 late forces retroactive tax-identifier collection with payout holds, so data collection belongs in onboarding thresholds.

advances_thesis.how: Names a failure the corresponding design rule prevents.

sections.heading: The Chief Architect's View
sections.controlling_idea: At group scale, transactions raise four standing decisions: decide the pivot per profile with named owners, share the platform only among the profiles that use it, treat the provider as a strategic dependency, and measure trust and money together.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the chapter into governance a group Chief Architect can apply.

transition_in.introduces: The standing decisions that prevent them at group scale.

flow.rationale: Whether to pivot comes before what to share, which comes before how to manage the provider beneath it, and measurement comes last because it judges the other three.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At group scale, transactions raise four standing decisions that prevent the failure modes.
Decide the pivot per profile and record it in the marketplace profile register as configuration, with no category given protected payment without named owners for disputes, reconciliation and DAC7.

transition_in.introduces: The first: whether and where.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Share the transaction platform only among the profiles that use it, with country parts as adapters and the order model, ledger and case model shared.

evidence.what: Safe Deal serves goods in Tradeyard's countries; Motorvane and Hearthly use only the shared layers beneath it.
evidence.shows: Shows sharing scoped to the profiles that pivot.

transition_in.introduces: What to share among those that do.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Treat the provider as a strategic dependency: keep the order, the ledger and the verification outcome in your own systems with provider identifiers as references, and plan for separability.

transition_in.introduces: The provider beneath it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Measure trust and money together, so a rising protected share with falling phishing shows the pivot working and a rising take rate with rising unmatched items shows it borrowing from the future.

transition_in.introduces: How to judge the whole pivot.

sections.heading: Questions to Ask
sections.controlling_idea: Ten questions test a transaction design against the chapter, from the four conditions and who holds the money to release, reservation, traceability, disputes, DAC7, provider exit, brand phishing and switching off.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the reader a design-review audit drawn from every section.

transition_in.introduces: Questions that test whether they are met.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ten questions, introduced by a one-line lead-in, test whether a transaction design meets the chapter's conditions, ownership rules and obligations.

conclusion.heading: From Transactions to Monetization
conclusion.synthesis: The four conditions and the six contexts are one decision seen from two sides: the conditions say where the platform's presence removes a fear that stops sales, and the contexts are what it costs to carry that fear once the platform has taken it on; each forum decision needed both, and Safe Deal's clearing balance is what taking on the fear without the second half produced.
conclusion.so_what: A 'let's go transactional' proposal is answered with two questions, not one: do all four conditions hold for this country and category, and can the platform that will carry it explain every amount from order to bank.

callback.to: The twenty-year classifieds bargain in the opening paragraph (the platform finds the buyer and the parties settle the money).
callback.how: The reader now sees the bargain as right for some categories and wrong for others, and knows what breaking it obliges the platform to own.

takeaway.content: Break the classifieds bargain only per category and only with the ledger and dispute desk in place; then weigh the transactional line against the other revenue models in monetization-models.

hand_off.carries_over: Protected payment adds a revenue line, but only one of several and usually not the largest.
hand_off.introduces: The other ways a listing marketplace earns, which charge for access to attention rather than a share of the sale, each with its own system of record and liquidity cost.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapter's conditions, platform, decisions and questions.
transition_in.introduces: What they amount to together, back at the opening bargain.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The classifieds bargain the chapter opened with is right for some categories and wrong for others: the four conditions say where the platform removes a fear, the six contexts are the cost of carrying it, and the forum's decisions and the clearing balance show that both halves are needed.

evidence.what: Portugal passed the conditions but waited for the ledger; the car payment and the deposits failed conditions no platform can change; Safe Deal took on the fear without the ledger and produced €2.3 million unmatched.
evidence.shows: Shows the two halves working together, which no single section states.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A proposal to go transactional is therefore answered with two questions, whether all four conditions hold and whether the platform can explain every amount, and only a yes to both turns buyer protection from a liability into a product.

transition_in.carries_over: The two halves of the decision.
transition_in.introduces: The two questions a reader puts to any proposal.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Protected payment adds a revenue line, but only one of several and usually not the largest, so monetization-models compares it with the models that charge for attention.

transition_in.carries_over: The transactional line judged on its own.
transition_in.introduces: The other revenue models it competes with.
